steps.tx: A traumatic **fracture shaft femur** requires massive kinetic energy transfer, typically generated by motor vehicle accidents or industrial crushing. Fractures occur along the cylindrical cortical diaphysis between five centimeters distal to the lesser trochanter and eight centimeters proximal to the adductor tubercle. Large deforming muscular vectors from the iliopsoas, gluteal muscles, and adductors produce predictable fragment displacements.
steps.say: A femur shaft fracture requires high kinetic energy, like a highway crash or fall from height. It spans between five centimeters below the lesser trochanter down to eight centimeters above the adductor tubercle. Powerful muscle forces from iliopsoas, abductors, and adductors displace the bone fragments predictably.

steps.tx: The loose fragment in the middle of this fracture is not incidental detail. A **butterfly fragment** forms when bending forces split a cortical wedge from the femoral shaft, marking high energy injury and telling the surgeon the fracture will not behave like a simple transverse break. Displacement on both views shows how powerfully the surrounding muscles pull fragments once continuity is lost. Winquist Hansen grading uses cortical contact between main fragments to judge whether length can hold without fixation.
steps.say: A butterfly fragment marks a high energy bending injury of the femoral shaft. Cortical contact between the main fragments judges whether length will hold without fixation.

vis.alt: Anteroposterior and lateral radiograph style views of a midshaft femoral fracture with displacement and a cortical butterfly fragment.
vis.caption: Displaced midshaft femoral fracture fragments are shown on two views, with a butterfly cortical fragment between them. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Internal **haemorrhagic shock** represents an immediate life threat because closed femoral shaft fractures bleed one thousand to fifteen hundred milliliters of blood directly into the muscular thigh compartments. Blood loss is exacerbated by ongoing motion of bone spikes tearing the muscular arcade. Rapid application of a Thomas splint restores limb length, reduces thigh volume, and limits haematoma expansion.
steps.say: Closed femur fractures can lose over one liter to fifteen hundred milliliters of blood into the thigh, triggering hemorrhagic shock. Bone fragments continue to lacerate muscle vessels until stabilized. Applying a Thomas traction splint immediately aligns the bone, reduces thigh volume, and stems blood loss.

left.title: Blood Loss Dynamics
points: 1000 to 1500 mL blood loss in closed break
Over 2000 mL in open or bilateral fractures

steps.tx: The **Winquist-Hansen classification** categorizes femoral shaft fractures based on cortical comminution to predict rotational stability. Type I has minimal or no comminution. Type II features a butterfly fragment smaller than fifty percent of the cortical width. Type III exhibits a comminuted butterfly exceeding fifty percent with tenuous cortical contact. Type IV denotes segmental comminution with complete loss of cortical contact.
steps.say: The Winquist-Hansen system grades comminution. Type one has zero to tiny comminution. Type two has a butterfly fragment under half the bone width. Type three has a large butterfly exceeding fifty percent of the cortex. Type four is segmental comminution with total loss of cortical contact.

steps.tx: A critical post-traumatic complication is **fat embolism** syndrome, occurring twenty-four to seventy-two hours following injury due to systemic intravasation of marrow fat droplets. The classic clinical triad presents with progressive respiratory distress, neurological depression ranging from confusion to coma, and petechial hemorrhages distributed across the anterior chest, axillae, and subconjunctival spaces.
steps.say: Fat embolism syndrome develops one to three days after femur trauma as bone marrow droplets shower the pulmonary and systemic circulation. Look for the classic triad of sudden hypoxia, confusion, and a petechial rash over the upper chest, axillae, and conjunctiva. Early surgical fixation dramatically cuts this risk.

left.title: Major Diagnostic Criteria
points: Petechial rash in axilla and neck

right.title: Minor Diagnostic Criteria
points: Fat globules in urine or sputum

steps.tx: The definitive surgical gold standard is **intramedullary nailing** using an antegrade reamed interlocking nail. Reaming induces endosteal blood flow stimulation and deposits osteoinductive autologous bone graft at the fracture gap. Static interlocking screws placed proximally and distally preserve length, control rotation, and allow immediate axial weight-bearing, achieving union rates exceeding ninety-eight percent.
steps.say: Reamed interlocking intramedullary nailing is the gold standard for adult femur fractures. Reaming delivers osteogenic bone dust straight to the fracture line. Static interlocking screws lock in length and rotation, permitting early weight bearing and achieving union in ninety-eight percent of patients.

quiz.q: What is the expected internal blood loss from an isolated closed femoral shaft fracture?
quiz.explain: A closed femoral shaft fracture typically loses 1000 to 1500 mL of blood into the surrounding thigh muscles, predisposing the patient to hypovolaemic shock.

quiz.q: Which clinical feature constitutes part of the classic triad in fat embolism syndrome?
options: Petechial rash over the chest and conjunctiva
Isolated lower limb swelling and erythema
quiz.explain: Fat embolism syndrome classically presents with hypoxaemia, cerebral neurological changes, and a characteristic petechial rash over the non-dependent skin of the neck, chest, and conjunctiva.
